role_and_message.evidence: The M concept still explains why nearby low-resolution views can provide enough detail to supervise distant rendering.

panel_and_object_coverage.evidence: Both camera centers and image planes, patterned scene strip, two blue ground-truth frusta, one green render frustum and three red intersections remain.

labels_math_and_numbers.evidence: Near/Far camera and low-resolution ground truth/high-resolution render labels retain their original identities.

connections_and_direction.evidence: Two blue ground-truth arrows identify near and far frusta; the green render pointer identifies the narrower distant render frustum. All frusta share the original scene intersection and appropriate camera origin.

visual_encodings.evidence: Blue remains ground truth, green remains render and red remains marked scene/image-plane intersections; relative near/far sampling geometry is retained.

examples_and_data.evidence: This is a qualitative schematic without empirical photographs or calibrated measurements. Camera/frustum topology, ray boundaries and three red points were checked directly.

unsupported_additions.evidence: The new headline and final selective-super-resolution statement are exactly supported by Fig3 caption and Sec3.2/4.1.

complete_visible_content.evidence: All original conceptual elements, labels and pointer tips remain visible. Schematic dimensions are not interpreted as measured distances.

remaining_limitations: Source example/schematic scope and original resolution remain. Semantic fidelity is separate from visual quality and scientific validation.
caption:
Figure 3. Disparity in high-frequency ground truth informa-
tion across different views. Low-resolution ground truth from
near cameras provides high-resolution information for rendering
distant views, reducing the need for additional generated detail
in those views. Conversely, super-resolution is needed in views
where no other camera provides higher-resolution information.
